statement: To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
heath_proof: Let AB be the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let BC be an annex to AB; therefore AC, CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which fulfil the given conditions. [X. 77] I say that no other straight line can be annexed to AB which fulfils the same conditions. For, if possible, let BD be so annexed; therefore AD, DB are also straight lines incommensurable in square which fulfil the given conditions. [X. 77] Since then, as in the preceding cases, the excess of the squares on AD, DB over the squares on AC, CB is also the excess of twice the rectangle AD, DB over twice the rectangle AC, CB, while twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by a rational area, for both are rational, therefore the squares on AD, DB also exceed the squares on AC, CB by a rational area: which is impossible, for both are medial. [X. 26] Therefore no other straight line can be annexed to AB which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole fulfils the aforesaid conditions; therefore only one straight line can be so annexed.

10.83
**Statement:** To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let BC be a straight line annexed to AB, so that AC is the whole straight line and CB the annex. By 10.77, AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a second straight line BD, different from BC, can also be annexed to AB with the same properties: AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, and twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational (10.77). Since BC and BD are unequal, let BD be the greater; then C lies between B and D, so AC is a part of AD and CB a part of DB, whence AD is greater than AC and DB greater than CB (CN5). Consequently the square on AD is greater than the square on AC and the square on DB is greater than the square on CB, the lesser square being a part of the greater (CN5); so the sum of the squares on AD, DB exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB by some area. Call this excess E.

**Step 3.** Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB (2.7). Likewise, since AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB (2.7).

**Step 4.** By Step 2, the squares on AD, DB are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with E. Replacing each sum of squares by the equal area found in Step 3 (CN1), twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB and E. Subtracting the common square on AB from both (CN3), twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with E. Thus twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the same area E by which the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB.

**Step 5.** E is a rational area. Let K be the square on the rational straight line set out. Twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K (D10.1.4). Hence twice the rectangle AD, DB is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.12). Now twice the rectangle AD, DB is the whole composed of the two parts twice the rectangle AC, CB and E, and this whole is commensurable with the part twice the rectangle AC, CB; therefore the parts are commensurable, that is, E is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.15). Since twice the rectangle AC, CB is commensurable with K, E is also commensurable with K (10.12), and therefore E is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 6.** Therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is a medial area, exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is also a medial area, by the rational area E. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible.

**Step 7.** Hence no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB so as to be incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and to make with the whole the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational. Therefore to a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one such straight line can be annexed. Q.E.D.
